Why is a point of efficiency worth more the closer a converter is to 100%?
column2: Loss is \(P_{out}(1 - \eta)/\eta\), so \(dP_{loss}/d\eta = -P_{out}/\eta^2\): near 100% each point removes about 1% of \(P_{out}\) of heat. Going from 96.5% to 97.5% cuts the loss by about 29%, and that heat is what the cooling and the box size are built around.

column1: What is the best efficiency an LDO can reach, and why?
column2: \(\eta_{LDO} = V_{out}I_{out}/[V_{in}(I_{out} + I_Q)] \le V_{out}/V_{in}\): the pass device drops the difference voltage at the full load current. From 3.6 V to 1.2 V it cannot beat 33%.

column1: Why can a switching converter be lossless in principle?
column2: An ideal switch has either zero voltage across it or zero current through it, so it dissipates nothing; inductors and capacitors only store energy. The switch node's average is \(DV_{in}\), and an LC filter keeps the average while rejecting the switching harmonics.

column1: State the two rules every switching topology must obey.
column2: Rule 1: never connect a capacitor directly to a source at a different voltage (it loses \(\tfrac12C\Delta V^2\) whatever the resistance). Rule 2: never interrupt an inductor's current (it would demand an infinite voltage); every converter provides a second path, a diode or a synchronous switch.

column1: How much energy is lost charging a capacitor from 0 to \(V\) through a resistor from a fixed source? How do you lose less?
column2: \(\tfrac12CV^2\), independent of \(R\): the source supplies \(CV^2\) and only half is stored. Charging in \(N\) equal steps loses \(\tfrac12CV^2/N\); charging through an inductor (resonantly) can lose almost nothing.

column1: Where does a converter with loss \(P_0 + aI + RI^2\) peak in efficiency?
column2: At \(I^* = \sqrt{P_0/R}\), where the conduction loss \(RI^2\) equals the fixed loss \(P_0\). Below it the fixed loss dominates (light-load efficiency falls), above it conduction does.

column1: When should a multiphase converter add a phase?
column2: Going from \(N\) to \(N + 1\) phases adds \(P_0\) but cuts conduction from \(RI^2/N\) to \(RI^2/(N + 1)\); it pays above \(I = \sqrt{N(N + 1)P_0/R}\). Shedding phases at light load is the reverse.

column1: How does efficiency limit power density?
column2: If a box can reject \(q\) watts of heat per unit volume, \(\rho = P_{out}/\text{Vol} \le q\,\eta/(1 - \eta)\): 19 times \(q\) at 95%, 99 times at 99%. Halving the loss nearly doubles the achievable density, and a density figure means nothing without its box.

column1: Size a hold-up capacitor.
column2: It must supply \(P_{bus}t_{hold}\) while falling from \(V_1\) to \(V_2\): \(C = 2P_{bus}t_{hold}/(V_1^2 - V_2^2)\). Energy goes as \(V^2\), so the converter's minimum input voltage sets how much of the stored energy is usable.

column1: What are volt-second and charge balance?
column2: In periodic steady state an inductor's current and a capacitor's voltage return to their starting values each cycle, so the average inductor voltage and the average capacitor current are both zero. Every DC conversion ratio follows from them.

column1: Give the buck's conversion ratio and inductor ripple in CCM.
column2: \(V = DV_{in}\); \(\Delta i_L = (V_{in} - V)DT_s/L = V(1 - D)/(f_sL)\). Designers usually choose \(L\) for a ripple ratio \(r = \Delta i_L/I\) of about 0.2–0.4.

column1: Give the buck's output voltage ripple.
column2: Capacitive: \(\Delta v = \Delta i_L/(8f_sC)\), from the triangle of charge above the average. ESR adds \(\Delta i_L R_{ESR}\); the two peak at different times, so the total is less than their sum.

column1: What RMS currents does a buck impose on its parts?
column2: Inductor \(I\sqrt{1 + r^2/12}\); high side \(\sqrt D\) and low side \(\sqrt{D'}\) times that; input capacitor \(\approx I\sqrt{D(1 - D)}\), worst (\(I/2\)) at \(D\) = 0.5. RMS current, not average, sets heating and capacitor ratings.

column1: How do conduction losses enter the buck's steady-state model?
column2: \(V = DV_{in} - IR_{eq}\) with \(R_{eq} = DR_{HS} + D'R_{LS} + R_L\), so \(\eta = 1/(1 + R_{eq}/R)\). The loop raises \(D\) slightly to hold the output.

column1: Why do low-voltage bucks use synchronous rectification?
column2: A diode loses about \(D'V_FI\), which is a large fraction of a 1 V output's power; a MOSFET in its place loses \(D'I^2R_{LS}\), far less at these voltages. The price is dead-time control to avoid shoot-through.

column1: When does a buck enter discontinuous conduction, and what changes?
column2: When the load falls below \(I_{crit} = \Delta i_L/2\), equivalently \(K = 2L/(RT_s) < 1 - D\), the inductor current reaches zero and (with a diode or diode emulation) stays there. The gain then depends on load: \(M = 2/(1 + \sqrt{1 + 4K/D_1^2})\).

column1: What is pulse-frequency mode (PFM) and what does it cost?
column2: At light load the converter delivers fixed charge packets only when the output needs them, so switching loss scales with load and efficiency stays high. The costs are a variable switching frequency (noise can land in sensitive bands) and larger ripple.

column1: How does minimum on-time limit a buck?
column2: The on-time is \(DT_s = V/(V_{in}f_s)\); with a controller's minimum on-time \(t_{min}\), \(f_s \le V/(V_{in}t_{min})\). Large step-down ratios such as 48 V to 1 V force low frequencies or two stages.

column1: Give the boost's conversion ratio and inductor current.
column2: \(V = V_{in}/D'\) and \(I_L = I/D'\): the inductor carries the input current, larger than the load current by the boost ratio.

column1: Why can a real boost not reach arbitrarily high gain?
column2: With inductor resistance \(R_L\), \(V/V_{in} = (1/D')/(1 + R_L/(D'^2R))\). The gain peaks at \(M_{max} = \tfrac12\sqrt{R/R_L}\) when \(D' = \sqrt{R_L/R}\); beyond it more duty cycle lowers the output, and efficiency \(1/(1 + R_L/(D'^2R))\) collapses.

column1: Why is a boost's output ripple larger than a buck's?
column2: The diode delivers current to the output only during the off-time, so the output capacitor alone supplies the load during the on-time: \(\Delta v = ID/(f_sC)\), driven by pulsed current.

column1: What does an inverting buck-boost give, and what does it cost?
column2: \(V = -(D/D')V_{in}\), stepping up or down with inverted polarity. The switch and diode block \(V_{in} + \lvert V\rvert\) and carry \(I/D'\), so its stress per watt is the highest of the basic three.

column1: Compare SEPIC and Ćuk converters.
column2: Both give \(\lvert V\rvert = (D/D')V_{in}\) with two inductors and a coupling capacitor. SEPIC is non-inverting with a continuous input current; Ćuk inverts but has both input and output currents continuous.

column1: When is a boost in discontinuous conduction?
column2: When \(K = 2L/(RT_s) < K_{crit} = DD'^2\). Its gain is then \(M = \tfrac12(1 + \sqrt{1 + 4D^2/K})\), set by load; at light load the duty cycle needed for the same output falls.

column1: Why is a power-factor corrector a boost?
column2: It must draw sinusoidal current from a rectified line and make a DC bus above the line's peak. A boost's input current flows through its inductor continuously, so it can be shaped; its duty cycle sweeps over the line cycle, approaching 1 near the zero crossings.

column1: How does a flyback transfer energy, and what is its ratio?
column2: Its coupled inductor stores energy in \(L_m\) while the switch is on and releases it to the secondary when off. In CCM, \(V = (V_{in}/n)\,D/D'\) with \(n = N_1/N_2\).

column1: What voltage must a flyback's switch block?
column2: \(V_{in} + nV\) (input plus reflected output), plus a spike from the leakage inductance, which an RCD or active clamp limits.

column1: How much energy does a flyback's RCD clamp absorb per cycle?
column2: \(E_c = \tfrac12L_{lk}I_{pk}^2\cdot V_c/(V_c - V_R)\), more than the leakage energy because the magnetizing inductance keeps feeding the clamp until the leakage current falls. A tight clamp (close to \(V_R\)) raises the multiplier.

column1: Give the forward converter's ratio and its reset limits.
column2: \(V = DV_{in}/n\). A reset winding \(N_3\) returns the magnetizing energy: \(D_{max} = 1/(1 + N_3/N_1)\) and the switch blocks \(V_{in}(1 + N_1/N_3)\) (0.5 and \(2V_{in}\) for \(N_3 = N_1\)).

column1: Why must a forward converter's core be reset every cycle?
column2: The on-time applies volt-seconds that ramp the magnetizing current and flux; unless an equal and opposite volt-second product is applied before the next cycle, the flux walks up cycle by cycle until the core saturates.

column1: What sets a transformer's flux swing in a converter?
column2: \(\Delta B = V_{in}DT_s/(N_1A_e)\). In a forward converter \(V_{in}D = nV\) is fixed by the output, so the normal swing does not depend on input voltage, but a transient at high input and maximum duty can more than double it.

column1: Why isolate, and what does it cost?
column2: For safety (reinforced insulation from mains), to break ground loops, and to make large step ratios with a turns ratio. The costs are a transformer, a feedback path across the barrier, clearance and creepage distances, and leakage energy.

column1: Why do bridges replace flybacks at high power?
column2: In a bridge each switch blocks only the input voltage and the transformer is driven in both directions, using the core's full flux range; a flyback's switch sees input plus reflected voltage and, since all the energy passes through one inductor, carries \(I_{pk} = 2P/(V_{in}D)\) in DCM: several times a bridge switch's current (Example 22-04.7).

column1: Why is an inductor's core gapped?
column2: The gap's reluctance dominates, so \(L = \mu_0N^2A_e/(g + \ell_e/\mu_r)\) barely depends on the material's variable \(\mu_r\), the core saturates at a higher current, and the energy is stored in the gap.

column1: What is a gapped core's effective permeability?
column2: \(\mu_e = \mu_r/(1 + \mu_rg/\ell_e)\); a small gap reduces \(\mu_r\) of thousands to an effective value of tens.

column1: How do you find a core's saturation current and stored energy?
column2: \(B = LI/(NA_e)\), so \(I_{sat} = B_{max}NA_e/L\). The energy is \(\tfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0}A_e(g + \ell_e/\mu_r) \approx B^2V_{gap}/(2\mu_0)\): the gap volume sets how much energy a core can hold.

column1: How does eddy-current loss scale, and what does it imply for materials?
column2: \(p_{eddy} = \pi^2f^2B_{pk}^2t^2/(6\rho)\): as \(f^2\) and lamination thickness squared, and inversely with resistivity. Silicon steel works at 50–60 Hz; ferrites, ceramics of high resistivity, work at hundreds of kilohertz as solid blocks.

column1: What are Steinmetz's equation and the iGSE for?
column2: \(P_v = kf^\alpha B_{pk}^\beta\) fits sinusoidal core-loss data. The iGSE extends it to converter waveforms: for a triangle, \(P_v = k_i(\Delta B)^\beta f^\alpha[D^{1 - \alpha} + D'^{1 - \alpha}]\), which rises at extreme duty cycles because of the fast edge.

column1: What is the skin depth, and its value in copper at 100 kHz?
column2: \(\delta = \sqrt{\rho/(\pi f\mu_0)}\): about 0.21 mm at 20 °C and 0.24 mm at 100 °C. Conductors much thicker than δ carry current only near their surface.

column1: What does Dowell's formula say about multilayer windings?
column2: The AC-resistance factor grows with the layer count \(M\) and with \(\Delta = h/\delta\): for small Δ, \(F_R \approx 1 + (5M^2 - 1)\Delta^4/45\). Proximity effect, not skin effect, dominates multilayer windings; interleaving primary and secondary cuts it.

column1: What is the area-product method?
column2: The core must fit both the flux and the copper: \(A_p = A_eW_A \ge LI_{pk}I_{rms}/(K_uJB_{max})\). Choose a core above that, then turns \(N = LI_{pk}/(B_{max}A_e)\) and the gap.

column1: Where is a transformer's total loss minimized?
column2: With core loss \(a\Delta B^\beta\) and copper loss \(b/\Delta B^2\), at \(\Delta B_{opt} = (2b/(\beta a))^{1/(\beta + 2)}\), where \(P_{fe}/P_{cu} = 2/\beta\), not 1. The minimum is flat, so nearby turn counts cost little.

column1: What sets a transformer's leakage inductance?
column2: The magnetic energy in the space between windings: \(L_{lk} = (\mu_0N^2\,\text{MLT}/b_w)(h_p/3 + d + h_s/3)\). Interleaving halves the field's peak, cutting the winding terms to a quarter and the insulation term to half, so leakage falls by 2–4× depending on which dominates.

column1: Estimate hard-switching overlap loss.
column2: With linear ramps, \(P_{ov} = \tfrac12VI(t_{on} + t_{off})f_s\). It grows with voltage, current, transition time and frequency, which is why high-voltage converters chase fast switches or soft switching.

column1: Why does a hard turn-on in a half bridge cost \(Q_{oss}V\) rather than \(E_{oss}\)?
column2: The switch turning on dumps its own stored \(E_{oss}\), and the bus charges the other switch's output capacitance through it, losing \(Q_{oss}V - E_{oss}\). The total is \(Q_{oss}V\).

column1: What is reverse-recovery loss and which devices avoid it?
column2: A conducting PN diode stores minority charge \(Q_{rr}\) that must be swept out when the opposite switch turns on, costing about \(Q_{rr}V\) per edge. GaN HEMTs have no body diode and no \(Q_{rr}\); SiC MOSFET body diodes have small \(Q_{rr}\); silicon superjunction devices have large \(Q_{rr}\).

column1: What does gate drive cost?
column2: \(P_g = Q_gV_{drv}f_s\): each cycle moves the gate charge from the driver supply and dumps it. Gate resistance changes where the heat goes, not the total.

column1: What is the optimal switch size, and what figure of merit decides it?
column2: \(P(R) = I_{rms}^2R + (RQ)V_{drv}f_s/R\) is minimized at \(R^* = \sqrt{(RQ)V_{drv}f_s}/I_{rms}\), where conduction and charge losses are equal: \(P_{min} = 2I_{rms}\sqrt{(RQ)V_{drv}f_s}\). Only a lower \(R\cdot Q\) lowers the minimum, which grows as \(\sqrt{f_s}\).

column1: Why can a MOSFET run away thermally?
column2: \(R_{DS(on)}\) rises with temperature, so heat raises loss, which raises heat. With \(R(T) = R_{25}[1 + k(T - 25)]\), no steady state exists once \(R_{th}I^2R_{25}k \ge 1\).

column1: What is the ZVS condition?
column2: During the dead time, the inductor current must swing the switch node by moving \(2Q_{oss}\): \(t_{tr} = 2Q_{oss}/I \le t_d\), so \(I \ge 2Q_{oss}/t_d\). Then the switch turns on at zero voltage and the turn-on overlap and \(Q_{oss}V\) losses vanish.

column1: How does an LLC converter achieve ZVS?
column2: Its magnetizing current, peaking at \(I_{m,pk} = V/(8L_mf_s)\) in a half bridge, flows at each switching instant and swings the node. ZVS needs \(I_{m,pk} \ge 2Q_{oss}/t_d\), an upper limit on \(L_m\); low-\(Q_{oss}\) GaN allows a larger \(L_m\) and less circulating current.

column1: Why do wide-bandgap devices have lower on-resistance?
column2: A wider bandgap gives a higher critical field (at 10¹⁶ cm⁻³: about 0.3 MV/cm for Si, 3.1 for 4H-SiC, 4.9 projected for GaN, a GaN figure that is [Contested]), so a thinner, more heavily doped drift region blocks the same voltage. Baliga's limit puts specific on-resistance as \(1/\mathcal E_c^3\).

column1: Give the buck's control-to-output transfer function.
column2: \(G_{vd}(s) = V_g/(1 + sL/R + s^2LC)\): a double pole at \(f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\) with \(Q = R\sqrt{C/L}\). Above \(f_0\) its phase approaches −180°.

column1: Why does a boost have a right-half-plane zero, and what does it limit?
column2: Raising the duty cycle first cuts the time the inductor feeds the output, so the output dips before the larger inductor current arrives. The zero at \(D'^2R/(2\pi L)\) adds phase lag with rising gain, so crossover must stay well below it, typically a fifth or less.

column1: Why does a voltage-mode buck need a type-III compensator?
column2: Above \(f_0\) the plant's phase is near −180° and the integrator adds −90°, so the compensator must supply more than 90° of lead at crossover; two zeros and two poles provide up to 180°.

column1: How does the k-factor method place a type-III compensator?
column2: Required boost \(B = \text{PM} - 90° - \varphi_p\); \(k = \tan((B/2 + 90°)/2)\); zeros at \(f_c/k\), poles at \(kf_c\); then \(\omega_I\) sets \(\lvert T(j\omega_c)\rvert = 1\), using \(\lvert G_c(j\omega_c)\rvert = (\omega_I/\omega_c)k^2\).

column1: What limits a converter's crossover frequency?
column2: The averaged model fails approaching \(f_s/2\), and switching ripple must not be amplified into the duty cycle, so \(f_c\) is a fraction of \(f_s\); a boost's RHP zero and a digital controller's delay lower it further.

column1: What is subharmonic instability in peak current mode, and its fix?
column2: A current perturbation changes by \(\alpha = -m_2/m_1\) each cycle; above \(D\) = 0.5, \(\lvert\alpha\rvert > 1\) and it grows, alternating. A compensating ramp \(m_a\) gives \(\alpha = -(m_2 - m_a)/(m_1 + m_a)\); \(m_a > (m_2 - m_1)/2\) stabilizes, and \(m_2/2\) is common.

column1: Estimate a regulator's load-step deviation.
column2: Until the loop responds, the output capacitor supplies the step: \(\Delta V \approx \Delta I/(2\pi f_cC)\). Faster crossover or more capacitance reduces it.

column1: What phase does a digital controller's delay cost?
column2: A delay \(t_d\) costs \(360° \times f_ct_d\) at crossover. A 1 µs delay at 40 kHz costs 14.4°, so delay often limits the achievable bandwidth.

column1: What does a PMIC contain?
column2: Several bucks and LDOs (and often boost, charger and load switches), sequencing and soft start, a digital interface for voltage and mode control, monitoring and protection, on one chip that powers every rail of an SoC.

column1: Why feed an LDO from a buck, and what does it cost?
column2: The buck does the large step efficiently and the LDO cleans the ripple for a noise-sensitive rail. The chain's efficiency is \(\eta_{buck}V_{out}/V_{mid}\), so the intermediate voltage should sit just above the LDO's dropout.

column1: Where should a buck hand over from PFM to PWM?
column2: Where \(P_f + RI^2 = V_{in}I_q + \alpha I + R_pI^2\). Below it PFM's load-proportional switching loss wins; above it PWM's lower conduction loss wins. Auto mode adds hysteresis to avoid chattering.

column1: How do you estimate a wearable's battery life?
column2: Sum each state's regulated energy divided by its converter efficiency, plus the PMIC's own quiescent draw: \(E_{day} = \sum P_it_i/\eta_i + V_{bat}I_qT_{day}\). Short high-power bursts (radio, display) often dominate a day.

column1: What does dynamic voltage scaling demand of the regulator?
column2: Ramping the rail at slew \(S\) needs extra current \(CS\) into the output capacitance. Going down in PFM, the rail falls only as fast as the load discharges it, so PMICs often force PWM during transitions.

column1: What does adaptive voltage scaling save?
column2: It trims each chip's supply to the minimum that chip needs instead of a worst-case guardband; dynamic power scales as \(V^2\), so the saving is \(1 - (V_2/V_1)^2\).

column1: What does soft start control, and what does it not save?
column2: It limits inrush current \(C\,dV/dt\) when a rail or domain turns on. It does not save energy: charging the capacitance through a switch dissipates \(\tfrac12CV^2\) whatever the ramp rate.

column1: When is power gating worth it?
column2: When the domain stays off longer than \(t_{be} = (CV^2 + E_{state})/P_{leak}\): recharging costs \(CV^2\) from the supply plus any state save and restore.

column1: What sets a cell's voltage and its theoretical capacity?
column2: Voltage \(E = -\Delta G/(nF)\) from the reaction's free energy; capacity \(q_{th} = F/(3.6M)\) mAh/g per mole of lithium stored in host mass \(M\): 372 mAh/g for graphite (LiC₆).

column1: Describe the standard equivalent-circuit cell model.
column2: An OCV that depends on state of charge, \(V_{OC}(z)\), in series with an ohmic \(R_0\) and one or more RC pairs for diffusion and charge transfer: \(v = V_{OC}(z) - iR_0 - v_1\), with \(dz/dt = -i/Q\).

column1: Why does a cell deliver less capacity at high current or in the cold?
column2: Discharge ends when the terminal reaches cutoff, \(V_{OC}(z_{end}) = V_{cut} + IR\). Higher current or higher (cold) resistance reaches cutoff at a higher OCV, stranding charge; the OCV curve's shape decides how much.

column1: Describe CC/CV charging and the CV phase's time constant.
column2: Constant current until the terminal reaches \(V_{max}\) (at \(V_{OC} = V_{max} - I_{cc}R\)), then constant voltage while the current decays as \(I_{cc}e^{-t/(RC_{eff})}\), with \(C_{eff} = Q/(dV_{OC}/dz)\), until \(I_{term}\).

column1: Why does doubling the charge current not halve the charge time?
column2: A larger \(I_{cc}\) reaches \(V_{max}\) earlier, at a lower SOC, leaving more charge for the CV phase, whose time constant \(RC_{eff}\) does not change. Hence "0–50% in 15 minutes" headlines.

column1: Compare linear and switching chargers.
column2: A linear charger drops \(V_{in} - V_{bat}\) at the charge current, so its efficiency is \(V_{bat}/V_{in}\) and it heats most when the battery is low. A switching (buck) charger runs at about 90% or more and suits high currents.

column1: How does a fuel gauge track state of charge?
column2: Coulomb counting integrates current but drifts with offset and gain errors; OCV readings at rest re-anchor it. Two rest points around a counted charge give the present capacity, \(Q_{max} = \Delta q/(z_1 - z_2)\).

column1: Why does calendar fade slow over time?
column2: The SEI film grows only as fast as reactants diffuse through it, \(dL/dt = D'/L\) with \(D'\) an effective diffusivity, so \(L = \sqrt{2D't}\): capacity loss goes roughly as \(\sqrt t\). High SOC and temperature speed it.

column1: What do JEITA charging guidelines do?
column2: They define temperature bands: reduced current in the cold (to avoid lithium plating) and a lower charge voltage when warm (4.10 V instead of 4.2 V in the warm band), with no charging outside the limits.

column1: Why are AI racks moving from 48–54 V to 800 V or ±400 V DC?
column2: For fixed power and conductor, \(P_{loss} = P^2R/V^2\): loss, or copper for a given loss, falls as \(1/V^2\). At rack powers of about 120 kW today and 800 kW–1 MW specified (as of Nov 2026), 54 V needs impractical busbar copper.

column1: What does distributing a load along a busbar do to its loss?
column2: With loads tapped uniformly, the current falls linearly along the bar and the loss is \(I^2(2R)/3\), a third of the loss if all the current ran the full length.

column1: How do conversion efficiencies and PUE combine?
column2: \(P_{IT} = P_{chip}/\prod\eta_i\) over the in-rack stages (rack PSU onward), and the facility draws \(P_{IT}\) times its PUE, which already covers the UPS and cooling. Quoting one stage's efficiency says little about grid power per chip watt.

column1: Why interleave regulator phases, and when does ripple cancel fully?
column2: Each phase carries \(I/N\); the summed ripple shrinks and appears at \(Nf_s\): \(\Delta I_\Sigma = (V_{in}T/L)(ND - m)(m + 1 - ND)/N\). It vanishes when \(ND\) is an integer; at low duty cycles cancellation is partial.

column1: What does a load line (AVP) buy?
column2: Letting the output fall as \(V_{ID} - R_{LL}I\) uses the whole voltage window for each transient instead of half, and lowers the voltage, and power, at heavy load.

column1: What is a target impedance?
column2: \(Z_t = \Delta V_{allowed}/\Delta I_{max}\), to be met by the PDN from DC to the highest frequency in the load current: the regulator up to its bandwidth, then bulk, ceramic, package and die capacitance.

column1: What causes the first droop, and how big is it?
column2: Package inductance against on-die capacitance resonates at \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\), tens of megahertz. A fast step \(\Delta I\) droops by \(\Delta I\sqrt{L/C}\) a quarter period later; ESR near \(Z_0/2\) damps it best.

column1: Why move power stages under the processor?
column2: At a kiloampere, tens of micro-ohms of lateral plane resistance cost tens of watts and tens of millivolts. Vertical delivery shortens the high-current path to millimetres; it does not remove the package and die loop that sets the first droop.

column1: How does DC compare with three-phase AC per conductor?
column2: \((P_{DC}/2)/(P_{AC}/n_c) = n_cV_{DC}/(2\sqrt3V_{LL}\cos\varphi)\); the answer depends on the voltages, conductor count and power factor assumed, which is why published comparisons differ.

column1: How does a machine convert energy?
column2: A conductor carrying \(i\) in a field feels \(F = Bi\ell\); moving at \(v\) it develops \(e = B\ell v\). Together \(ei = T\omega\): the power absorbed by the back EMF equals the mechanical power.

column1: Describe a PM DC motor's speed–torque line.
column2: \(E_a = k\omega\), \(T = kI_a\), \(V = E_a + I_aR_a\), so \(\omega = V/k - (R_a/k^2)T\): no-load speed \(V/k\), stall torque \(kV/R_a\). Without mechanical loss its efficiency is \(E_a/V\).

column1: How do three windings make a rotating field?
column2: Windings 120° apart carrying balanced currents produce \(\tfrac32B_m\cos(\theta - \omega t)\), a constant field rotating at synchronous speed \(n_s = 120f/P\) rpm.

column1: What is slip and why must an induction motor have it?
column2: \(s = (n_s - n)/n_s\). Rotor currents are induced only if the rotor moves relative to the field; they run at \(sf\) and produce the torque.

column1: How does an induction motor's air-gap power split?
column2: \(P_{ag} = 3I_2^2R_2/s\): \(sP_{ag}\) is rotor copper loss and \((1 - s)P_{ag}\) becomes mechanical power; torque \(= P_{ag}/\omega_s\). Running at high slip is inherently inefficient.

column1: What sets an induction motor's maximum torque and where it occurs?
column2: \(s_{max} = R_2/\sqrt{R_{th}^2 + (X_{th} + X_2)^2}\) and \(T_{max} = 3V_{th}^2/(2\omega_s[R_{th} + \sqrt{R_{th}^2 + (X_{th} + X_2)^2}])\). \(T_{max}\) does not depend on \(R_2\), so rotor resistance moves the peak without changing its height.

column1: How does a synchronous motor's power depend on its angle and excitation?
column2: \(P = 3VE_f\sin\delta/X_s\), with pull-out at δ = 90°. Field current sets \(E_f\) and so the reactive power: under-excited it absorbs VArs, over-excited it supplies them, like a synchronous condenser.

column1: What is constant V/f control, and what happens above base speed?
column2: Flux is proportional to \(V/f\), so holding \(V/f\) keeps flux and torque per ampere constant as the drive changes frequency. Above rated frequency the voltage cannot rise, flux falls and torque falls as \(1/n\): the constant-power field-weakening region.

column1: How much line voltage can a three-phase inverter make?
column2: Sine-triangle PWM: \(V_{LL,rms} = (\sqrt3/2\sqrt2)mV_{dc} \approx 0.612mV_{dc}\). Third-harmonic injection or space-vector PWM raises the maximum to \(V_{dc}/\sqrt2\), 15.5% more.

column1: Why do variable-speed drives save so much on fans and pumps?
column2: Flow goes as speed and pressure as speed squared, so power goes as speed cubed: 60% speed takes about 22% of full power, while throttling at full speed saves little.

column1: Why use per-unit, and how do you change base?
column2: With \(I_b = S_b/(\sqrt3V_b)\) and \(Z_b = V_b^2/S_b\), transformer turns ratios disappear and quantities fall in narrow ranges. \(Z_{pu,new} = Z_{pu,old}(V_{b,old}/V_{b,new})^2(S_{b,new}/S_{b,old})\).

column1: Why do overhead lines all have similar reactance per kilometre?
column2: Inductance \((\mu_0/2\pi)\ln(D/r')\) and capacitance \(2\pi\varepsilon_0/\ln(D/r)\) depend on geometry only logarithmically, so 60 Hz reactances cluster around 0.3–0.5 Ω/km.

column1: What is surge-impedance loading?
column2: SIL \(= V_{LL}^2/Z_c\), \(Z_c = \sqrt{L/C}\): the load at which the line's series reactive absorption equals its shunt generation. Below SIL a line raises its voltage; above, it sags.

column1: How do real and reactive power flow between two buses?
column2: \(P = (V_1V_2/X)\sin\delta\), set mainly by angle, flowing from leading to lagging bus. \(Q\) flows from higher to lower voltage magnitude, set mainly by the magnitudes; maximum transfer is \(V_1V_2/X\).

column1: Estimate a line's voltage drop.
column2: \(\Delta V \approx (RP + XQ)/V\); on high-X/R lines reactive power dominates, which is why reactive compensation controls voltage. The quadrature drop \((XP - RQ)/V\) adds about its square over \(2V\).

column1: Give the three-phase and single-line-to-ground fault currents.
column2: Three-phase: \(I_f = V_f/Z_1\), fault MVA \(S_b/Z_{1,pu}\). Single-line-to-ground: \(I_a = 3V_f/(Z_1 + Z_2 + Z_0)\), larger than the three-phase fault when \(Z_0 < Z_1\).

column1: What sets the initial rate of change of frequency after a generator trips?
column2: Inertia alone: \(\text{RoCoF} = -\Delta Pf_0/(2HS)\) with stored energy \(HS\). Inverter-based generation adds no inertia unless programmed to, so RoCoF rises as it replaces machines.

column1: How does droop share a load change, and where does frequency settle?
column2: Each governor responds \(\Delta P_g = -(S/R)(\Delta f/f_0)\); the frequency settles at \(\Delta f_{ss} = -\Delta P/(\sum S_i/(R_if_0) + D)\). Secondary control (AGC) then restores nominal frequency over minutes.

column1: Why do grid operators now worry about datacenter loads?
column2: Datacenters are large enough to matter to the bulk system. In July 2024 a fault sequence led about 1,500 MW of datacenter load to transfer to backup within seconds, a sudden loss of load; as of Nov 2026, NERC has issued alerts and proposed registering large loads.
